speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In general, the questions raised by Ms Poh Li San and Ms Carrie Tan deal with the role of women in the national defence of Singapore.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Similar issues were raised during the debate in this House on the White Paper on Singapore Women's Development and my reply today will address the general theme, as well as specific queries.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The proposal to enlist women into National Service (NS) is not new.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In fact, it was debated as early as 1967, when NS was first introduced into this House.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It was during the debate on the National Service (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: To the then-Member of Parliament for Tiong Bahru, Mr Lee Teck Him, Dr Goh Keng Swee replied that we had not reached the stage where mandating NS for women was necessary.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But it is important to state clearly why we hold to this position, so that this House and Singaporeans understand how we have sustained the strong support for NS and built up a credible SAF.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The principal considerations which go to the heart of Ms Carrie Tan's questions, that men, but not women, were mandatorily enlisted when NS began, had less to do with gender equality than the pressing need to quickly build up a military to defend Singapore.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The British had announced in 1967 that they would pull out all forces from Singapore by April 1971 and that precipitated a live challenge.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: An SAF had to be built from scratch and expeditiously, because there were clear and present dangers that threatened our very existence as a fledgling nation.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Dr Goh Keng Swee and his officials and the SAF pioneers' first preference was, actually, not NS conscription, but an army formed by regulars, men and women.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They did not want to deal with the potential problems of NS – turning civilians into soldiers, equity, defaulters, deserters, training injuries and even deaths, among them.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But, a regular army would not have been sufficient to protect Singapore.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, NS was started and this House subsequently passed the Enlistment Act in 1970.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In fact, Mr Lee Kuan Yew wrote in his memoirs "From Third World to First: The Singapore Story", and I quote, "I was keen to have our women do National Service as Israeli women did, because that would reinforce the people's will to defend themselves.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But Keng Swee did not want his new Ministry to carry this extra burden.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As the other Ministers in Defco" – meaning Defence Council – "were also not anxious to draft our women, I did not press my point." "An extra burden" – our founding leaders and Dr Goh Keng Swee were honest and professional in their assessment.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Building up SAF with male conscripts alone was difficult.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I quote for you Dr Goh's words: "At that time, we were just beginning; SAFTI was just ongoing, probably producing its first or second output of non-commissioned officers (NCOs) and officer cadets.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We had an acute shortage of training officers and commanders from NCOs upwards, and the thought of raising a huge NSF army just made us shrink from the responsibility." We are used to the image of Singapore's Founding Fathers.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In fact, behind the brave exterior of SAF pioneers, laid doubts and insecurities.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Enlisting women would have been an "extra burden" that they did not want to take on.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Today, NS is well-accepted and SAF functions well.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, it is hard to imagine that Dr Goh Keng Swee and the SAF pioneers could have felt overwhelmed – so much so that, today, I think we take NS for granted.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But, despite the enormous challenge that our founders had, they persisted, overcame and we enjoy the fruits of their labours.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In 1975, full-time NS could be extended to bring in NSFs for the Singapore Police Force (SPF) as well as for the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) in 1981.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Despite falling birth rates, SAF has maintained operational readiness with reduced manpower through the same use of technology and optimising resources.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I have given many examples in this House of how this transformation has produced today's modern SAF that is more mechanised, motorised, lethal and effective, despite smaller numbers of soldiers.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Having reached this position of strength, should we, for the sake of gender equality, introduce NS for women?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I think that is the question that some people have put forth.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Some proposed this idea during the debate on the White Paper, including to deploy these NS conscripts as nurses or teachers.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I think there are distinct pitfalls, if conscription is implemented for any other reason than the critical need of military defence, whether it is for men or women.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Compared to 1967, when we introduced NS, Singapore remains one of the few countries that NS is accepted, working well and enjoys strong public support.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And the main reason that we have this virtuous state of affairs is that we have kept the mission of NS clearly focused on the critical need for national defence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The primary reason for enlistment into SAF must remain to train a soldier who is able to defend Singapore and to repel, if not defeat, an enemy who wants to invade our country.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Likewise, enlistment into the Police and SCDF must be based on the national need for homeland security and emergency services.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This stark raison d'être of NS to fight and defend our country and ensure its security is the foremost consideration that must undergird the mandatory enlistment of all National Servicemen.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is very far off from the proposals to conscript women to serve in roles such as caregivers and healthcare workers, or to send a powerful signal of gender equality.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These are inadequate justifications or reasons to mandate that someone must suspend individual liberties as a civilian, give up two years of his or her life; and, if they do not, they go to jail, as our Courts have sentenced NS defaulters.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Further, the societal cost of enlisting women into NS now would far outweigh the benefits.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Women would be delayed in their entry into the workforce.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The immediate effect will be an accentuated decline in the size of our local workforce and the reduction of household incomes.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Even if women are enlisted for non-military NS roles to augment our healthcare and social services, it may make manpower shortages in other industries worse.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Over the long term, it will impose a great cost not only on women themselves, but also on their families, children and spouses, and society as a whole.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Is that cost justified to send a signal or to reverse stereotypes?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I think most Singaporeans would say no, too, from a security perspective.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But, if Singapore was ever threatened with an existential threat by an aggressor and have a sudden and great need to boost our military, I am certain that MINDEF and SAF would call on the Government of that day to enlist not only women, but even teenagers and older men into military service to defend and save Singapore.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Ukrainians did exactly this when their homeland was invaded.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They required women employed in a wide range of professions, aged between 18 and 60, to register for possible military conscription.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Young men and the elderly, who were well past their retirement age, also volunteered to fight on the frontlines to protect their country.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In fact, I had a few emails from retired Singaporean males who offered to come back into the SAF, I am not sure why, when Ukraine was invaded.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I sent them a polite reply and said, "we do not need you, yet." There was even a report published in Reuters in February 2022 of a 79-year-old Ukrainian woman, who was filmed at a training ground handling a Kalashnikov assault rifle.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But we are not there today and hope never to be.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In considering NS for women, we should not inadvertently downplay or dismiss the already significant contributions that women do make in national defence and security by serving as Regulars and volunteers.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Ms Poh Li San asked about the measures undertaken to expand the roles that Regular servicewomen can serve in SAF.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Our Regular servicewomen currently serve in vocations, such as Infantry, Artillery, Armour, Combat Engineers, Pilots and Naval Officers, amongst others.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In addition, more than 500 women have been trained and deployed as SAF volunteers (SVs) in a variety of roles since 2015.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Indeed, servicewomen within SAF hold their own and many punch above their weight.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Progression to senior ranks for all personnel is based on merit, capability and aptitude, as it is for all soldiers.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We hope to see this figure increase as the proportion of servicewomen in SAF continues to grow.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We need to look no further than Members in this House as good examples – Ms Gan Siow Huang and Ms Poh Li San.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As our first female Brigadier-General in SAF, Ms Gan took command of the Air Power Generation Command, which is the largest formation in the Republic of Singapore Air Force (RSAF).

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Ms Poh also started her career in RSAF as a helicopter Search and Rescue pilot and was the Flight Commander of 125 Squadron.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: She was also the first female full-time Aide-de-Camp to the late President, Mr SR Nathan.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Outside SAF, women serve as Regulars in SPF and SCDF, and contribute to our national defence and security.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For example, other than serving in SPF as a Police Inspector in the 1990s, Ms Sylvia Lim was appointed as a member of the Advisory Council on Community Relations in Defence, ACCORD, from 2012 to 2020, where she maintained support for our national defence among the community and business groups.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Ms Poh Li San also asked about SAF's efforts to continue expanding the proportion of servicewomen in SAF and those who hold senior leadership positions.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have stepped up our recruitment of women because SAF wants more women to join our ranks and will make it more attractive for them to do so.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For example, we facilitate flexible work arrangements, such as part-time or job-sharing and telecommuting, where possible, without compromising operational readiness.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have also implemented policies to help our servicemen and women take better care of their loved ones with childcare and parent care leave, and counselling services to support their well-being.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This provides dedicated focus to review policies and create a conducive and progressive workplace experience for our servicewomen.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This is the basis of the social compact and individual responsibility for NS, and those who do not comply are dealt with harshly.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Historically, SAF started the conscription of males and is able to defend Singapore today against potential aggressors and provide adequate deterrence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The cost on women themselves, their families and society does not justify enlisting women into NS for those reasons.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Women are already contributing to nation-building as Regulars and volunteers.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: SAF and Home Team welcome more women to pursue full-time careers or join their volunteer units.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: My second question is on flexible work arrangements (FWAs) for our servicewomen.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Beyond no-pay leave and current FWAs, what else can MINDEF offer our servicewomen, so that they can spend a few years to start their young families and still come back to the force to contribute?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Thankfully, and I suppose, expectedly, we are counter cyclical when it comes to the economy.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Our recruitment has been fairly successful and our attrition quite low.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But, despite that, we recognise that there are falling numbers.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As I had said, even with the decline in manpower and our birth rates, we have been able to keep SAF's effectiveness and operational readiness.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In terms of how we are adapting SAF and MINDEF to be a choice workplace for Singaporeans, it is an HR challenge – let me frame it that way.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In other words, despite being a military, how do you attract and recruit Singaporeans – males, females – who want to join you?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We recognise that COVID-19 has precipitated a number of changes, which will not go back to status quo ante.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have peculiar security needs, so, working from home is harder.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In lieu of that, let me give an example.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And just like the whole-of-Government and Civil Service, we are seeing how work away from office – rather than near home or at home – is very much, we believe, an entrenched concept.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If you try to fight it, you will not become an attractive recruiter as an organisation.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We are going to embrace it, but see how it works.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Speaker, I generally agree with what the Minister for Defence has explained on the women's role in the defence of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, I think it is also an appropriate instance now to raise the issue: is the sharing of the burden of the defence of our country now being reviewed, in view of the fact that we have a rising population, but we continue to have a declining number of male enlistees?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, is there a review being done as to how we can ensure that the sharing of the burden of the defence of this country is being done properly?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Who and which group is he referring to?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: What I am referring to is, the burden of defending this country must be shared, in my opinion, by all the citizens of this country.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: That is why we are here today, talking about what are the roles women can play, whether they can play a bigger role in the defence of this country.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, at the same time, we also know that our population is increasing, but there are still not enough male enlistees in our SAF.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, why is that situation allowed to be continued?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Speaker, I have gone to great lengths in describing that SAF, even from its inception, had made use of technology and optimising resources, so that we can build a credible and strong SAF, even despite declining enlistees.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, the assertion by Mr Leong Mun Wai goes completely against what I have said in the last 15 minutes.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: He either does not believe me or thinks that SAF is not credible, and, therefore, the rest of his questions are not germane.
